name: Questioning Your Own Sources
title: Questioning Your Own Sources
answer: Questioning your own sources is the habit of auditing the evidence base of a review you are writing or have already published, rather than trusting the citations you have accumulated. It covers whether each cited work exists, whether it is primary or a report of someone else's finding, whether it actually says what your sentence claims, and whether it has been corrected or retracted since you read it. It also covers the quieter problem of selection, meaning which sources you found, which you stopped looking for, and which you left out. The practice applies to a narrative review as much as to a systematic one, though the formal record keeping differs.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Questioning your own sources is the habit of auditing the evidence base of a review you are writing or have already published, rather than trusting the citations you have accumulated. It covers whether each cited work exists, whether it is primary or a report of someone else's finding, whether it actually says what your sentence claims, and whether it has been corrected or retracted since you read it. It also covers the quieter problem of selection, meaning which sources you found, which you stopped looking for, and which you left out. The practice applies to a narrative review as much as to a systematic one, though the formal record keeping differs.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on ordinary reference infrastructure: a reference manager such as Zotero, DOI resolution to the publisher record, library databases and preprint servers, and the retraction and correction notices that publishers issue. On this site, the library holds 135 research papers and 12646 extracted claims, and each claim can be traced back to the paper it came from, because content links to the original paper rather than to a search tool. That traceability is what makes an audit possible at all, since a claim with no route back to its source cannot be checked. Where a source sits behind a paywall, the abstract alone is usually not enough to confirm what the paper reports.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: In practice you take each claim in your draft and open the source, then read the passage that is supposed to support it, checking the study design, the sample and the direction of the effect rather than the title. You separate primary sources from secondary ones, because a review that cites another review is repeating a summary and can inherit its errors. You check the current status of each work against retraction and correction notices, and you note the venue and whether it was peer reviewed. A common shortcut is to sample a portion of the reference list, perhaps the most load bearing citations, and verify those closely, keeping a written record of what you changed and why.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The risks are citation error, misrepresentation of a source's finding, and the persistence of retracted work in later literature, all of which can travel for years once published. Provenance matters in both directions: you need to know where a claim came from, and a reader needs to be able to follow your citation back to the same place. Copyright and licensing shape how much of a source you may quote or reproduce, and the terms of a database or publisher platform govern how you may reuse its records. If an error is found in your own published review, the usual route is a correction or an erratum rather than a silent edit. This is a description of practice, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Automated claim extraction and source matching are making it cheaper to check a large reference list, and several tools now flag retractions, citation mismatches and papers that no longer resolve. Language models are being used to screen and summarise candidate sources, which raises the same question in a new form, since a summary is not the source and can be confidently wrong. The direction of travel is toward provenance metadata travelling with the claim, so that a reader can see not only the paper but the passage and the version it came from. Open peer review and versioned preprints push in the same direction, though they also multiply the versions a reviewer has to keep straight.
